lesson.title: The Bonds That Hold a Molecule Together
lesson.summary: Intramolecular forces are the strong attractions, chemical bonds such as covalent, ionic, and metallic bonds, that hold the individual atoms of a molecule or compound together internally.
lesson.body:
Intramolecular forces are the forces found inside a single molecule or formula unit, the attractions responsible for actually holding its atoms together as one connected structure. This category is really just another name for chemical bonds themselves: covalent bonds, in which atoms share electron pairs, ionic bonds, in which oppositely charged ions attract each other in a lattice, and metallic bonds, in which metal cations are held in a shared sea of delocalized electrons. Whichever type is present, intramolecular forces are what define the molecule or compound's identity, its formula, and its basic chemical properties.

The defining feature of intramolecular forces is their strength, which is best measured through bond energy, the amount of energy required to break one mole of a particular bond in the gas phase. Breaking intramolecular forces is a chemical change: snapping a covalent bond in a water molecule to separate it into hydrogen and oxygen atoms requires a substantial input of energy, several hundred kilojoules per mole, and produces new chemical species entirely different from water. The single O-H bond in water, for example, requires roughly 460 kilojoules per mole to break, a quantity representative of covalent bond strength generally, which typically ranges from around 150 to over 800 kilojoules per mole depending on the specific bond and whether it is single, double, or triple.

This magnitude matters because it sets the scale against which every other force in this chapter should be judged. A useful mental anchor is that intramolecular bond energies are commonly one to two orders of magnitude larger than the energies associated with attractions between separate molecules; where covalent bonds require hundreds of kilojoules per mole to break, the intermolecular attractions introduced elsewhere in this chapter typically require only a few to several tens of kilojoules per mole to overcome. Keeping that scale difference in mind prevents a common confusion: melting ice or boiling water changes the physical state of H2O without breaking a single O-H covalent bond, because those processes only need to overcome the comparatively weak attractions between separate water molecules, not the strong intramolecular bonds within each one.

Because intramolecular forces are what define a substance chemically, changing them always means a chemical reaction has occurred, new bonds broken and new bonds formed, producing genuinely different substances with different formulas. This is the essential contrast that sets up the next concept in this chapter: intramolecular forces determine what a molecule is, while the forces that act between molecules determine how those molecules behave in bulk, as a liquid, solid, or gas, without changing what they fundamentally are. Recognizing which category a given force belongs to, whether it is holding atoms together within a molecule or holding whole molecules together as neighbors, is the key skill that the next section builds on directly.
